one_liner: Full-spec YAML 1.2/JSON parser and emitter in C, with 3.0-3.6x yaml-cpp's parse throughput in fkYAML's benchmark.
what_it_does: A C library that parses and emits YAML 1.2 and JSON, keeps YAML 1.1 compatibility, and passes the full official YAML test suite, according to its repo description. It has three API layers. The first is a libyaml-style event stream (fy_parser_parse). The second is a mutable document tree with path queries and an emitter whose formatting you control (fy_document_*, fy_node_*, fy_emit_*). New in 1.0 are the fy_generic value layer and reflection-driven YAML<->C-struct serdes. It is not a drop-in for yaml-cpp: you work with opaque C handles, errors come back as NULL/-1 plus a diagnostics object, and scalars arrive as (pointer, length) text that you convert yourself.
how_it_is_fast: The scanner is zero-copy. Tokens are 'atoms' holding start/end marks into the input: files are mmap'd, in-memory strings are referenced without copying, and escape/fold processing happens only when someone asks for the text. Freed tokens, events and parser-state objects go onto per-parser recycling lists instead of back to malloc. Each mapping node can also carry an xxHash32-keyed hash table (an 'accelerator'), which makes key lookups and duplicate-key checks O(1) instead of a list scan. The core scanner has no SIMD: the SSE/AVX/NEON code in the tree belongs to the bundled BLAKE3 hasher, which keys the opt-in transparent parse cache. On a cache hit, that cache loads a serialized generic arena instead of re-parsing.
when_to_use: C or C++ code that needs full YAML 1.2 conformance (anchors, tags, complex keys, multi-document streams, JSON input) and wants about 3x yaml-cpp's DOM-parse throughput on small-to-medium documents.

Round-trip tools such as config editors, formatters and linters that must keep comments (FYPCF_KEEP_COMMENTS), original styles (FYPCF_KEEP_STYLE) and source markers, then re-emit with controlled indentation and quoting.
Large or streaming inputs where you do not want a tree at all: the event API walks the document without building one.

Processes that re-read the same large, rarely changing YAML/JSON files at every startup: the opt-in cache (FYPCF_ENABLE_CACHE) skips re-parsing unchanged content. The docs say it helps little for tiny or volatile inputs.
C codebases that want YAML decoded straight into native C structs (reflection API) or into a Python-like immutable value model (fy_generic).
when_not_to_use: When raw parse speed is the point. In the same fkYAML benchmark, fkYAML was 2.1-2.6x faster than libfyaml and rapidyaml 2.2-4.2x faster (for example 132-151 vs 36 MiB/s on ubuntu.yml). The project's own docs say it puts correctness ahead of raw speed.

Untrusted input on the v1.0.0-beta1 tag. Fuzzing since August 2026 produced dozens of now-closed reports: use-after-free, heap overflows, exponential-time alias/merge-key resolution (#347, #400) and quadratic mapping builds (#394). The fixes are on master, and no release has been tagged since beta1 (2026-08-13).

When you want idiomatic C++. There is no C++ wrapper, RAII or exceptions, and libfyaml-cpp.h is a C-preprocessor macro kit, not a C++ API. The generic layer's macros rely on C11 _Generic and GNU statement expressions, so treat generics and reflection as C-only.
MSVC (cl) builds that need generics, reflection or the parse cache. These need statement expressions, which only GCC, Clang and clang-cl provide, and the generic layer is also little-endian only.
Sharing one document across threads. The docs say the document subsystem is not designed for multithreaded processing; only the immutable fy_generic values can be read-shared without locking.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (CMake or Autotools; BUILD_SHARED_LIBS defaults ON; find_package(libfyaml) and pkg-config supported)
integration.dependencies: pthreads on non-Windows (required); bundled xxHash and BLAKE3; optional libclang/LLVM to author reflection metadata from C headers (not needed at runtime with packed blobs); optional libyaml for a compatibility mode
integration.min_toolchain: C11 compiler (CMake prefers gnu2x/c2x and falls back to gnu11); CMake 3.14+. MSVC needs /std:c17 plus /experimental:c11atomics. Generics, reflection and the parse cache need GNU statement expressions (GCC/Clang/clang-cl). libclang-based reflection needs CMake newer than 3.27.
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows (MSVC, clang-cl, MinGW; CI covers ubuntu, macos, windows incl. windows-11-arm); x86-64, x86, arm64, arm. The core parser needs no SIMD. The generic layer is little-endian only; the mremap allocator is Linux-specific (with mmap/malloc fallbacks).
integration.thread_safety: The document API is not designed for multithreaded processing (doc/intro.rst). fy_generic values are immutable and read-shareable without locks. The library ships a thread pool for parallel generic transforms. The rules for confining a parser or document to one thread are not documented.

gotchas: In v1.0.0-beta1, the tag that was benchmarked, the default (iterative) document builder never set up the mapping accelerators, so duplicate-key checks are quadratic. Issue #394 measured 26.4 s for a 20,000-key flat mapping with the default config vs 0.05 s with FYPCF_PREFER_RECURSIVE. It is fixed on master (commit 4a9346d, 2026-09-23) but not yet in a tagged release.

Input strings are referenced, not copied. Memory inputs keep the caller's pointer, and fy_parser_set_string's doc says the string must not go out of scope while the parser is active. To hand ownership to the document, use fy_document_build_from_malloc_string. fy_node_get_scalar returns a pointer and length that is not NUL-terminated; fy_node_get_scalar0 allocates a terminated copy.

Aliases and merge keys are not resolved unless you set FYPCF_RESOLVE_DOCUMENT or call fy_document_resolve. Before the September 2026 fixes, resolving crafted merge-key aliases could take exponential time.

From C++ with Clang/libc++, <libfyaml.h> pulls in <stdatomic.h>, which defines atomic_load and similar names as macros. The project's own C++ test says to include <libfyaml.h> before any STL header that reaches <atomic>, or to keep such headers out of that translation unit.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick libfyaml over fkYAML, rapidyaml or PipeYAML when you are writing C, or when you need its documented extras: comment- and style-preserving round-trips, a libyaml-style event API, YPATH queries, YAML<->C-struct reflection, or the on-disk parse cache. For plain fast parsing into a tree from C++, the same benchmark shows fkYAML at 2.1-2.6x and rapidyaml at 2.2-4.2x libfyaml's throughput.
verified_claims_summary: fkYAML's author, a third party, benchmarked this with Google Benchmark on a Ryzen 7 5800H under WSL2, using g++ 11.4.0 in a Release build with libfyaml built static at -O2. The timed call was libfyaml v1.0.0-beta1's fy_document_build_from_string with the default config against yaml-cpp 0.9.0, parsing in-memory ubuntu.yml (about 8.6 KiB, derived from time x throughput), citm_catalog.json and citm_catalog.yml. Results were 35.98 vs 10.12 MiB/s (3.6x), 50.71 vs 16.67 (3.0x) and 21.94 vs 7.31 (3.0x). It was a single run, and libfyaml's documents are never destroyed inside the timed loop while yaml-cpp's teardown is timed, which slightly favors libfyaml.
status_note: Actively maintained by its original author (commits through 2026-09-23, with a burst of fuzzing fixes in September 2026) and MIT-licensed, but 1.0 is still in beta, so build from a recent master commit rather than the v1.0.0-beta1 tag if you parse untrusted or large-mapping input.
